To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we developed multidimensional measures for diet by identifying seven patterns among 1.475 male and 750 female subjects; (2) the patterns are gender-specific; (3) no one pattern signified good compliance with all guidelines; (4) the best indicators of noncompliance with NCI guidelines were the high-fat patterns in both males and females and the low-cost patterns in females; and (5) we developed a method to measure diet that can be applied in other settings
the patterns of food use in our study population were not consistent with the NCI Dietary Guidelines and that high-fat patterns in men and the low-cost patterns in women were the most prevalent.
we developed seven gender-specific patterns of food use and found no one pattern that signified compliance with the National Institute of Health (NIH) Dietary Guidelines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of dietary patterns and their association with cancer risk.
the use of dietary patterns as a method of identifying subgroups within a population and with the use of patterns to examine compliance with dietary guidelines.
the identification and characterization of patterns in food use and their association with compliance with the NCI Dietary Guidelines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a need for more research on diet patterns in relation to cancer risk.
no single pattern is a good indicator of compliance with the NCI guidelines.
there is no single pattern that is a good indicator of compliance with all NCI guidelines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a diet that is low in fat, high in fiber, and moderate in alcohol and meat is associated with the lowest risk for most cancers.
there is no one pattern of diet that is optimal for health and that the best diet is one that provides a variety of foods.
a high-fat pattern was a poor predictor of compliance with NCI Guidelines, and that the low-cost pattern was a better predictor of poor compliance in women.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dietary patterns are a useful tool to assess diet quality and to examine compliance with dietary guidelines.
dietary patterns are more likely to reflect compliance with NCI Dietary Guidelines than individual food components.
the NCI dietary guidelines are not being followed by the majority of the population, and that there is a need for more effective dietary interventions.
